case_name: Gujarat Ambuja Cement Limited and Another v Union of India and Others
petitioner: Gujarat Ambuja Cement Limited and Another
facts: The appellant-writ petitioners are manufacturers of cement.

Cement manufacturing plants in the western region of the country had not been given linkage by the linkage committee to lift coal from collieries situated nearby which were within reasonable distance, but they were forced to take coal from collieries situated in Madhya Pradesh wherein the respondent authorities were requiring the collieries, treating them as premium collieries, to charge 10% extra on the price of every grade of coal supplied to consumers like the writ petitioners.
Coal was a controlled commodity being treated as an essential commodity' under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act').
The said scheme was continued in force by Section 16 of the Act.
Prior to the independence of the country, there was in force Colliery Control Orders, 1945, wherein as per clause 4 thereof, price for supply of coal to the consumers was controlled.
issues: Whether the charging of 10% premium on A,B,C and D grades of coal supplied by these premium collieries is discriminatory and violative of the right guaranteed under Article 14 of the Constitution of India.
Whether Union of India has no legal right to impose premium.
Whether Item No.20 of the impugned notification ultra vires the Constitution.
petitioner_arguments: The grievance of the present appellant-writ petitioners before the High Court was that though same quality of coal as comprised in grades A,B,C & D was being supplied by different collieries, 10% premium over price was being charged only by some of the collieries as per Item No.20.

According to the writ petitioners, there was no choice of colliery from which they had to purchase coal at the relevant time as their choice was fettered by the decision of the linkage committee compelling the writ petitioners to purchase coal from a particular colliery.
It was contended that premium is not a price and Central Govt. has no power to impose premium.
Various dictionaries were referred to us so as to bring home the meaning of the word 'premium'.
respondent_arguments: The contesting parties produced material in support of their respective cases.

A clear stand was taken by learned counsel for the respondents namely, Union of India, Coal Indian Ltd. a Govt. Company and South-Eastern Coal Fields Ltd. a Govt. company, which were supplying the disputed quantity and quality of coal to the consumers like the writ petitioners and the coal controller who was functioning under the Colliery Control Order that the grievance made by the petitioners was of academic nature as it was open to the consumers of coal concerned to lift coal from any colliery of their choice and it was not compulsory for such a consumer to indent coal for Their factory only from a premium colliery which was charging 10% extra price on the quality of the coal supplied to these consumers.
It was submitted that the coal being of proper quality as supplied by premium collieries, charging of 10% more by way of price of such coal was legally justified and was not arbitrary.
court_reasoning: The High Court noted in the impugned judgment that the main grievance of the writ petitioners was that they had no choice as far as the purchase of coal was concerned.

It was observed that since it is not necessary to dwell at length on this point, in view of the statement made at the Bar by the respondent's counsel, Sri Nair contention on this point as raised by the petitioners are virtually rendered pure academics.
holding: The petitions are, therefore, dismissed with no order as to costs.
cases_cited: Gujarat Ambuja Cement Limited and Another v Union of India
